claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in high-entropy alloys is governed by preferential surface segregation of high-oxygen-affinity elements.
Al, Cr, and Si are examples of high-oxygen-affinity alloying elements.
The segregating elements form a continuous, adherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous multi-principal-element alloy containing selected high-oxygen-affinity elements.
The controlled comparison reduces or substitutes the high-oxygen-affinity elements while holding other composition and processing variables constant.
Both alloy sets will be exposed isothermally to air at 900°C for the same duration.
High-oxygen-affinity elements preferentially migrate to the surface during high-temperature exposure.
At the surface, these elements react with oxygen to form a dense, adherent oxide layer.
The dense oxide layer inhibits further oxygen ingress.
Inhibiting oxygen ingress slows the oxidation reaction.
Insufficient concentrations of high-oxygen-affinity elements produce a discontinuous or porous oxide scale.
A discontinuous or porous oxide scale causes accelerated oxidation.
The alloy richer in high-oxygen-affinity elements will form a more continuous and adherent oxide scale than the reduced-element control.
The alloy richer in high-oxygen-affinity elements will show lower mass gain and oxide thickness than the control.
The alloy richer in high-oxygen-affinity elements will exhibit greater resistance to oxide spallation than the control.
The proposed mechanism applies in oxidative atmospheres while the protective oxide remains stable, suggested as below approximately 1000°C.
The mechanism may fail at extremely high temperatures or in non-oxidative environments.
Oxidation studies broadly support a role for high-oxygen-affinity elements in forming protective oxides.
Segregation and scale-formation kinetics in multi-principal-element alloys remain incompletely established by controlled experiments.
Similar oxidation behavior in both alloys, or formation of a comparably protective scale by the reduced-element control, would refute the hypothesis.
